Abstract: Masked Generative Image Transformers (MaskGIT) have emerged as a scalable
and efficient image generation framework, able to deliver high-quality visuals with
low inference costs. However, MaskGIT’s token unmasking scheduler, an essential
component of the framework, has not received the attention it deserves. We analyze
the sampling objective in MaskGIT, based on the mutual information between
tokens, and elucidate its shortcomings. We then propose a new sampling strategy
based on our Halton scheduler instead of the original Confidence scheduler. More
precisely, our method selects the token’s position according to a quasi-random,
low-discrepancy Halton sequence. Intuitively, that method spreads the tokens
spatially, progressively covering the image uniformly at each step. Our analysis
shows that it allows reducing non-recoverable sampling errors, leading to simpler
hyper-parameters tuning and better quality images. Our scheduler does not require
retraining or noise injection and may serve as a simple drop-in replacement for
the original sampling strategy. Evaluation of both class-to-image synthesis on
ImageNet and text-to-image generation on the COCO dataset demonstrates that the
Halton scheduler outperforms the Confidence scheduler quantitatively by reducing
the FID and qualitatively by generating more diverse and more detailed images.

ABSTRACT

and efficient image generation framework, able to deliver high-quality visuals with
low inference costs. However, MaskGIT’s token unmasking scheduler, an essential
component of the framework, has not received the attention it deserves. We analyze
the sampling objective in MaskGIT, based on the mutual information between
tokens, and elucidate its shortcomings. We then propose a new sampling strategy
based on our Halton scheduler instead of the original Confidence scheduler. More
precisely, our method selects the token’s position according to a quasi-random,
low-discrepancy Halton sequence. Intuitively, that method spreads the tokens
spatially, progressively covering the image uniformly at each step. Our analysis
shows that it allows reducing non-recoverable sampling errors, leading to simpler
hyper-parameters tuning and better quality images. Our scheduler does not require
retraining or noise injection and may serve as a simple drop-in replacement for
the original sampling strategy. Evaluation of both class-to-image synthesis on
ImageNet and text-to-image generation on the COCO dataset demonstrates that the
Halton scheduler outperforms the Confidence scheduler quantitatively by reducing
the FID and qualitatively by generating more diverse and more detailed images.
Our code is at https://github.com/valeoai/Halton-MaskGIT.

INTRODUCTION
We propose a new scheduler for Masked Generative Image Transformers (MaskGIT), an emerging
alternative for image generation that offers fast inference. In contrast to the Confidence scheduler
traditionally employed in MaskGIT, our Halton scheduler spreads the tokens spatially, minimizing
the correlation of tokens sampled simultaneously, maximizing the information gained at each step,
and ultimately resulting in more diverse and more detailed images.
Iterative methods for image synthesis, such as reverse diffusion (Betker et al., 2023; Peebles & Xie,
2023; Esser et al., 2024) or next-token prediction (Yu et al., 2022), brought significant advances
in image generation, where images have attained photo-realistic quality. However, those methods
impose a slow and costly inference process, and state-of-the-art methods require customizing the
scheduling for the generative process (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021).
MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022; 2023), a recent approach based on the Masked Auto-Encoder (He
et al., 2022) paradigm, offers much faster inference times and is readily integrated into multi-modal,
multitask, or self-supervised pipelines (Mizrahi et al., 2024). MaskGIT operates in a tokenized
space, representing an image as a grid of discrete values. The MaskGIT training process necessitates
masking a specified number of token values, letting the neural network predict their values. That
framework constitutes a classification task on the discrete values of the masked tokens.
For inference, MaskGIT begins with a fully masked grid and iteratively samples the tokens according
to a schedule. The scheduler aims to unmask as many tokens as possible per step to speed up the
overall process while preventing sampling errors that may arise when too many tokens are unmasked
in parallel.
We will show that the Confidence scheduler designed for MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022; 2023), which
unmasks the most certain tokens first, impacts the generated images’ diversity and quality. That
scheduler tends to select clustered tokens due to the high confidence of the area surrounding already
predicted tokens (Figure 3). That results in a low information gain per sampling step.
Grounded by a mutual information analysis, we introduce a novel deterministic next-tokens scheduler
that harnesses the Halton low-discrepancy sequence (Halton, 1964). Our scheduler builds upon
insights on the evolution of the entropy throughout the image generation process, aiming to spread
out the tokens to achieve uniform image coverage. No retraining nor noise injection is needed, and
the scheduler easily plugs in MaskGIT models without requiring further changes. Compared to the
traditional Confidence scheduler, we generate more diverse and higher-quality images, as visually
appreciable in Figure 1 and extensively evaluated in our experiments.
Our primary contribution is the Halton scheduler (section 3), a novel scheduler for MaskGIT, with
improved results without additional compute, data, or training constraints. Additionally, we present a
novel mutual information analysis that clarifies the scheduler’s role in MaskGIT (subsection 3.1).
That analysis motivates our choice of the Halton scheduler but is not limited to our specific design
and can be applied more broadly. We extensively evaluate our scheduler in the experiments presented
in section 4, encompassing both class-to-image and text-to-image generation tasks.

to improve each other. More recently, diffusion models (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021; Song et al.,
2020; Rombach et al., 2022) advanced the state of the art by reframing the problem as a simpleto-train denoising process. Concurrently, inspired by language modeling, auto-regressive image

another line of attack. While both diffusion and auto-regression have demonstrated the capacity to
achieve high-quality outputs, they are also prone to long inference times.

1981), is a deterministic sequence designed to uniformly cover a space with minimal clustering
or gaps, optimizing uniformity compared to random sampling. Among all the low-discrepancy
sequence improvements, the Scrambled Halton Sequence (Kocis & Whiten, 1997) improves the

The original MaskGIT uses the Confidence scheduler, which orders the tokens according to their
confidence scores. The analysis shows that this scheduler induces a low MI, leading to a poor sampling
process.

3.2
THE HALTON SCHEDULE
The Halton scheduler builds the schedule S by selecting, at each step s, the next set Xs of tokens to
unmask, according to a quasi-random, low-discrepancy Halton sequence. The Halton sequence is a
deterministic sequence that provides a uniform spread of points in a d-dimensional space, with minimal
clustering and maximal coverage.

More precisely, the Halton sequence H = {h1, h2, ..., H} is a sequence where each h is a d-dimensional
vector. The sequence is constructed by taking the inverse of the base-b representation of each integer,
and combining each dimension using a different base. For example, the d=2 case with bases b1 and b2
would produce points (h1, h2), with h1 being the inverse of the base-b1 representation of the integer,
and h2 the inverse of the base-b2 representation.

The schedule S is built by selecting, at each step s, the next token to unmask according to the order
defined by the Halton sequence. Specifically, the token at position s is determined by the order defined by
the Halton sequence, which ensures that the selected tokens are spread out across the image, avoiding
clustering and ensuring uniform coverage.

This scheduling approach does not require any retraining of the model, nor does it introduce any noise
during the sampling process. The scheduler simply plugs into MaskGIT, replacing the existing Confidence
scheduler, and is compatible with any tokenization that allows for uniform grid sampling.

3.3
ANALYSIS OF THE HALTON SCHEDULE
The Halton sequence is known to provide a low-discrepancy, deterministic sampling of the space, which
minimizes the correlation between tokens sampled in the same step and maximizes the information gained
at each step. This property is crucial for reducing the KL divergence between the product distribution
and the true joint distribution, as defined in equation (4).

The Halton sequence is particularly useful in high-dimensional spaces, where it maintains uniformity
across dimensions, which is essential for the effectiveness of the sampling process in high-resolution images.

3.4
COMPARISON TO THE CONFIDENCE SCHEDULE
The confidence scheduler assigns to each token a priority based on the model's confidence in the
token's reconstruction. Tokens with higher confidence are selected first, leading to a localized sampling
process that can result in lower MI per step. The Halton scheduler, on the other hand, selects tokens
in a way that spreads out the information across the image, leading to higher MI per step and thus
better overall sampling quality.

In Figure 1, the generated images using the Halton scheduler show higher diversity and better
perceived quality compared to the confidence-based approach. The FID scores across different datasets
demonstrate the improved performance, with the Halton scheduler consistently outperforming the
Confidence scheduler.

3.5
ADVANTAGES OF THE HALTON SCHEDULE
The Halton scheduler offers several advantages over the existing Confidence scheduler:

- No retraining is required, as the scheduler simply plugs into the existing model.
- No additional noise is introduced during the sampling process.
- The scheduler is deterministic, which makes it easier to analyze and reproduce.
- The Halton sequence provides a quasi-random, low-discrepancy ordering that ensures uniform
sampling across the image, avoiding clustered selections that reduce the MI per step.
- The scheduling process is computationally efficient, with a linear complexity relative to the number of
tokens to unmask.

3.6
IMPLANTATION IN MASKGIT
The Halton scheduler can be easily integrated into the existing MaskGIT framework. The only changes
needed are in the scheduler's algorithm, which now selects tokens according to the Halton sequence instead
of the Confidence scores. The rest of the process remains unchanged, so the scheduler is compatible with
any other components of the model, such as the tokenizer or the decoder.
